item.title: James Copenhaver, man shot at Trump Butler rally, dies of complications from injuries: report
item.description: James Copenhaver, who was wounded in the 2024 assassination attempt on President Donald Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania, has died, according to several reports.
item.content:encoded:
James Copenhaver, of Coraopolis, Pennsylvania, who was wounded in a failed assassination attempt on President Donald Trump in 2024, has died, according to several reports.

Copenhaver, in his mid-70s, was one of several people who attempted assassin Thomas Matthew Crooks shot at the Butler Farm Show complex outside Butler, Pennsylvania, after Crooks scaled the roof of a nearby glass manufacturing building and took aim at the then-presidential candidate.

GOP LAWMAKERS BLINDSIDED BY NEW REVELATIONS ABOUT TRUMP BUTLER SHOOTER: ‘AWFULLY STRANGE’

A person who answered a phone number connected to Copenhaver's family directed Fox News Digital to a Pittsburgh law firm for confirmation and further comment. 

The House Republican Conference also posted an obituary for Copenhaver on social media, saying he had died Thursday.

Ken Silva, a journalist who wrote a book about the assassination attempt, wrote on his website that a person close to Copenhaver's family also confirmed Copenhaver had died and had been dealing with permanent injuries, including bullet fragments still lodged in his body.

A lawsuit Copenhaver filed against the United States earlier this year alleged he was also required to undergo multiple surgeries.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Alaska has a voting system like no other state. Republicans worry it could cost them in November
item.description: Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan faces Mary Peltola in Alaska's ranked choice voting Senate race, complicated by a "Decoy Dan" candidate on the ballot.
item.content:encoded:
Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan is in the middle of an extremely competitive race as he seeks re-election this year in red-leaning Alaska in a midterm showdown that's one of roughly a dozen that will determine if the GOP keeps control of the Senate.

Working against Sullivan as he runs for a third six-year term in the Senate is not only a rough political climate facing Republicans but also Alaska's unique electoral system, which includes four candidates from an open primary advancing to the general election, as well as ranked-choice voting.

Alaska is the only state in the nation to have a "top four" primary system, where candidates advance regardless of party affiliation. And it's one of only two states, along with Maine, to use ranked choice voting for statewide and federal races.

Defenders of the system say it gives independent voters more choices, weakens party control, and encourages candidates to appeal beyond their base.

SEEING DOUBLE: THE SECOND DAN SULLIVAN ADVANCES IN ALASKA'S CRUCIAL SENATE SHOWDOWN

Alaska GOP chair Carmela Warfield, in social media posts, has repeatedly referred to the state's electoral system as a "MESS."

Veteran GOP strategist Mary Marslender told Fox News Digital, "It's hurting the Republican Party."

Sullivan is battling former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola. The two candidates combined received over 90% of the primary vote.

But also on the general election ballot is Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher and registered Republican that Marslender and supporters of the senator call "Decoy Dan."

A GOP-aligned group Americans for Public Trust claimed that the other Sullivan, who is not related to the senator, was working with Democrats to confuse voters. The Peltola campaign and Daniel J. Sullivan both denied the allegation. The Alaska Division of Elections disqualified him from the ballot but the decision was overturned first by an Alaska Superior Court judge and later by the state Supreme Court.

SIX FORCES THAT COULD HELP REPUBLICANS DEFY HISTORY IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS

There is also a third Republican on the Senate ballot: Gerald Heikes. He advanced to the general election when fourth-place primary finisher Democrat David Leslie withdrew from the race.

Marslender claimed that the current system has "become an easy way for the Democrats to game the system."

Pointing to Daniel J. Sullivan's inclusion on the general election ballot, she said "that never would have been allowed in the previous old system… but because there's an open primary, he was allowed to be on the ballot."

"Republican primary voters under the old system wouldn't have voted for him, and he wouldn't have been in there."

Marslender added that because of ranked choice voting - where voters rank candidates by preference and if nobody receives a majority of first-choice votes, additional counting rounds occur until someone reaches a majority - there's a perception that Republicans would unite around the incumbent senator in the general election.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

But she said in Alaska, which is the nation's largest and most remote state, "it's really hard to get a statewide message out" due to "the geographical challenges."

Alaskans for Better Elections, which supports the system, has been holding events to help voters better understand how it works.

"Alaska’s election system celebrates our independence, giving us the freedom to vote for the person who is best for the job," the group highlights on its website.

The Senate race wasn't the only contest impacted by the current system. There were also 11th-hour withdrawals that rocked the races for governor and the U.S. House, which also cast a shadow on the state's unique voting process.

Alaska voters get to weigh in when they cast general election ballots to either keep or scrap the current system.

Matt Schultz, a Democrat who suspended his congressional bid before the primary, supports keeping the system. But he told the AP, "We need to make things much more transparent and predictable and understandable by the general public so that we can truly have trust in our democracy again."

Republican Lesil McGuire and Democrat Tom Begich, former state lawmakers who were both eliminated in the primary for governor, defended the system.

"Let’s be clear: We would have faced challenges and might not have advanced in a traditional closed or semi-closed primary. Our election system was not designed to guarantee anyone a win. It was designed to solve a problem: elections in which a narrow, more partisan slice of voters decided the November ballot, resulting in hyperpartisanship that limited progress," they wrote in an opinion piece in the Anchorage Daily News.

They emphasized, "We don’t support our current system because it was good for us as candidates; we support it because it’s good for us as Alaskans."

item.title: NFL fines player nicknamed 'Juice' $14,926 for using a drinking celebration, calling it offensive
item.description: Kyle Juszczyk is appealing a $14,926 NFL fine for his 'drinking' TD celebration against the Dolphins, which the league called an offensive demonstration.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL, which has an official beer sponsor, an official drink sponsor, and allows clubs to sell and serve alcoholic beverages in its stadiums during games, has fined San Francisco 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk for using a play celebration that imitates him "chugging a beer."

Let this marinate for a moment.

It gets crazier.

TEXANS' AZEEZ AL-SHAAIR TO BE FINED ONCE AGAIN BY NFL FOR WEARING PRO-PALESTINIAN PERSONAL MESSAGE ON EYEBLACK

Juszczyk received a letter from the league this week informing him he is being fined $14,926 for celebrating a touchdown by giving the universal symbol of taking a drink.

The league told Juszczyk he violated Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, when he did an "imitation of chugging a beer" after scoring a touchdown at the 5:46 mark of the third quarter against the Miami Dolphins.

NFL RESTARTS SOCIAL JUSTICE MESSAGING WHILE BATTLING DOMESTIC ABUSE, DRUNK DRIVING AND PROSTITUTION ARRESTS

"Your imitation of chugging a beer constituted an offensive demonstration and could reasonably be construed as being in poor taste," the league's fine letter to Juszczyk reads in part.

The letter also said, "players are expected to conduct themselves in a manner that reflects positively on the game and is consistent with NFL standards of sportsmanship."

NFL FINES SAINTS AND COWBOYS $500K FOR PRACTICE BRAWL, BUT FIGHTS WON'T STOP UNLESS PLAYERS GET FINED

Further offenses, Juszczyk was warned, would result in an escalation of disciplinary action, up to and including suspension. Juszcyzk is appealing the fine, per a source.

Juszczyk scored his touchdown against the Dolphins, celebrated, and soon afterward the television broadcast cut to a Michelob Ultra beer commercial.

Not.

Making.

This.

Up.

The NFL has an official beer. Anheuser-Busch and its major brand, Bud Light, serve as the official beer and hard seltzer sponsor of the NFL under an agreement running through the 2026-27 season.

And as part of that deal, the beer has promotional agreements with more than two dozen current NFL players. The ads featuring the players are utilized across national content and campaigns.

So, yes, the fine that the NFL is trying to levy is thick with irony.

But there is more because this could be perhaps the craziest NFL story of the year: Juszczyk's nickname is "Juice."

When he makes a play for the 49ers at home, the crowd chants, "juuuuuuuuice."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

So, maybe, the guy wasn't pretending to chug a beer. Maybe the NFL, awash in beer sponsorships, assumed every time someone drinks, they are imbibing beer.

Juszczyk told ESPN, "I don't even drink beer," and added on his social media, "Can't make this stuff up."

The NFL also has an official juice agreement through Pepsico with Tropicana.

But the league drink police didn't assume the guy nicknamed Juice was imitating taking a drink of juice.

item.title: Women's college soccer team makes disturbing discovery in locker room ceiling
item.description: Jayson Barker allegedly hid in the ceiling above the Wilmington College women's soccer locker room and photographed players as they changed.
item.content:encoded:
An Ohio man was arrested after allegedly taking photos of members of a college women's soccer team while hiding in the ceiling above their locker room, according to local reports.

Jayson Barker, of Jeffersonville, faces nearly a dozen counts of voyeurism after being discovered inside the ceiling of the women's locker room at Wilmington College, WLWT-TV reported.

Officers with the Wilmington Police Department responded to the Scheve Athletic Center on the school's campus just before 9:40 p.m. local time Tuesday following reports that someone was photographing team members as they changed.

CALIFORNIA FOOTBALL COACH ARRESTED AFTER STUDENTS MAKE DISTURBING DISCOVERY AT SCHOOL

When officers arrived, they found Barker already being detained by Wilmington College Campus Safety personnel.

Investigators determined that Barker, who was working at the school as a contract custodial employee, had hidden himself in the locker room's ceiling area before being discovered by a member of the team.

SCHOOL EMPLOYEE ACCUSED OF SECRETLY FILMING 12 GIRLS IN CHANGING ROOM FACES NEW CHARGES

"The college's paramount concern is the safety and well-being of its students," the institution said in a statement to the news outlet. "We have been providing counseling and other support services for the affected students since Tuesday night and are taking measures to ensure that no student's safety or well-being is compromised. Also, the college continues to assist with law enforcement's investigation."

Barker is charged with 11 counts of voyeurism and is being held at the Clinton County Jail on a $22,000 cash surety bond. He is scheduled to make his next court appearance on Oct. 5.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Wilmington College, the Wilmington Police Department, and the Clinton County Sheriff's Office for further comment.

item.title: Hayden Panettiere's overdose shows fentanyl crisis 'doesn't discriminate,' Stanford psychiatrist says
item.description: Hayden Panettiere's fatal fentanyl overdose involved a lethal mix of opioids, benzodiazepines and quetiapine, a Stanford addiction expert says.
item.content:encoded:
Hayden Panettiere's fatal overdose is a stark reminder that the fentanyl crisis has not gone away, even as the United States makes genuine progress in reducing overdose deaths since peaking in 2022.

This week, the Greenville County Coroner's Office ruled that Panettiere died from the toxic effects of five drugs found in her system: fentanyl, 4-ANPP, Alprazolam, Methocarbamol and Quetiapine.

Dr. Anna Lembke, a Stanford psychiatrist and addiction medicine specialist, told Fox News Digital that while the circumstances surrounding the actress' death remain unclear, the combination of drugs in her system likely increased the risk of a fatal overdose.

"We don't know if she sought out fentanyl. We don't know if she had a counterfeit pill that had fentanyl in it. She might have been prescribed fentanyl for pain," Lembke said. "She was also on a benzo. We know combining benzos and opioids increases the risk of overdose of each of those medications separately. It looks like she was also on Quetiapine, a mood stabilizer, but also highly sedating in the mix."

HAYDEN PANETTIERE DEATH: DEA JOINS PROBE INTO WHAT HAPPENED TO LATE STAR

Lembke continued: "We don't know where she sourced it, but it does look like it was a lethal polypharmacy, including fentanyl, which on its own is an incredibly lethal drug."

The Cleveland Clinic defines polypharmacy as taking several medicines regularly, usually four or more.

While Lembke cautioned against drawing firm conclusions about what exactly led up to Panettiere's death, she said the tragedy underscores a broader reality: fentanyl remains a deadly threat that can affect anyone.

"This is still a very serious risk, and it's a risk that doesn't discriminate. Old and young, rich and poor, famous, not famous. Because of the increased access to these highly potent and potentially lethal drugs in the modern age, we're really all at risk for this problem," Lembke said.

Fentanyl, a synthetic opioid up to 50 times more potent than heroin, has transformed the nation's illicit drug supply over the past decade.

PRESLEY GERBER’S DEATH SPARKS QUESTIONS ABOUT OVERDOSE, WITHDRAWAL AND REHAB SAFETY

Deaths involving synthetic opioids, primarily illicitly manufactured fentanyl, began climbing sharply in 2014 and reached a record 73,838 in 2022, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse.

Fentanyl's potency is only part of what makes it so dangerous, Lembke said. Just as concerning is how trace amounts are concealed in counterfeit pills designed to look like legitimate prescription medications.

Lembke said a "very real risk" for young people, even those who aren't struggling with addiction, is that they're given a pill at a party that looks just like Xanax or Oxycontin, when it is in fact a counterfeit pill that contains a small amount of fentanyl.

"A single dose to an opioid-naive person could kill, which is why it's so important that we have data-informed discussions with young people in particular," she said.

"The kind of experimentation with drugs in their youth that their parents might've engaged in relatively risk-free...it's not risk-free anymore" for young adults, she added.

Lembke encouraged parents to get ahead of the issue by talking openly about drugs before their children encounter inaccurate or misleading information on social media.

If a parent or guardian recognizes their child has a substance-use disorder, Lembke said they should resist the impulse to brush it off as "normal teenage experimentation."

"These drugs are far too accessible and far too lethal to just leave it to hoping that it will be a passing phase the kid will outgrow," she said. "We know that the earlier we intervene with addiction-related problems, the more likely we are to reroute that person on a new path of life."

Lembke also offered a message to doctors, who she said should prescribe potentially addictive medications cautiously and closely monitor patients for signs of misuse.

As a practicing psychiatrist, Lembke routinely prescribes stimulants for ADHD, opioids for pain and benzodiazepines for insomnia and anxiety. But she said physicians have a responsibility to prescribe them in the lowest effective amounts for the shortest possible duration.

item.title: 'Unmasking a Monster': Golden State Killer series challenges timeline of Joseph DeAngelo's crimes
item.description: Joseph DeAngelo admitted to 50 rapes and 13 murders, but new testimony and unseen evidence suggest the Golden State Killer's toll is far higher.
item.content:encoded:
For four decades, Joseph DeAngelo hid in plain sight as the man authorities would eventually identify as the Visalia Ransacker, the East Area Rapist and, most famously, the Golden State Killer. But a new Fox Nation series is investigating whether his known crimes tell the whole story.

"Golden State Killer: Unmasking a Monster" re-examines DeAngelo’s violent past through exclusive testimony and never-before-seen evidence, asking whether his crimes began earlier than previously believed and, if so, what additional victims he left behind.

"There’s a possibility, and probably a high likelihood, that he committed way more crimes than we ever will know about," said Anne Marie Schubert, who served as the Sacramento County district attorney from 2015 to 2023.

NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS

DeAngelo was arrested in 2018 at 72 years old following a search of genealogy websites, bringing an end to a decades-long hunt. In 2020, he pleaded guilty to 50 rapes and 13 murders.

The four-part series challenges the established timeline of DeAngelo’s crimes, beginning with accounts of earlier assaults and controlling behavior. It goes on to re-examine evidence surrounding the murders of two teenage girls and explores whether DeAngelo framed others to evade capture.

FOX HOLLOW CORONER REVEALS WHY HE DOUBTS SUSPECTED SERIAL KILLER ACTED ALONE IN HUNT FOR ANSWERS

Later episodes examine his more than 50 attacks as the East Area Rapist and his transformation from serial rapist to serial killer.

The series also raises questions about crimes that remain unsolved, including the cases of Donna Richmond and Bess Snelling, featuring new statements from alleged victims and their relatives.

One survivor featured in the series recounts being violently raped when she was 12 years old. Another person of interest believes his mother was a victim of DeAngelo.

The final chapter examines perhaps the largest lingering question surrounding DeAngelo’s crimes — whether they actually ended in 1986, or whether he continued prowling, raping and killing before his arrest more than three decades later.

item.title: Nikole Hannah-Jones' friend sends Black son to private school after NYT writer has education regrets
item.description: Jenisha Watts says her own childhood in struggling schools convinced her to choose private school for her son over the path Nikole Hannah-Jones took.
item.content:encoded:
The Atlantic staff writer Jenisha Watts said Wednesday she plans to send her young Black son to private school, citing her own experience with struggling schools while choosing a different path from friend and 1619 Project creator Nikole Hannah-Jones, who recently confronted regrets about her daughter’s public school education.

Watts said in her Atlantic essay that Hannah-Jones’ experience helped convince her she could not make the same decision for her son.

"I could never make the choice she made," Watts said. "I know too well what can go wrong. I’m sending him to a private preschool, and I plan to apply for private kindergarten too."

Hannah-Jones, who previously said that scrutiny of her decision should also focus on Black children whose families cannot afford better options, responded directly to Watts in a new statement to Fox News Digital.

'THE VIEW' HOST SUNNY HOSTIN CLAIMS HER CHILDREN EXPERIENCED RACISM AT PRIVATE SCHOOLS

"I have a deep respect for Jenisha and all she has overcome," she said. "Our concerns and values as parents are always shaped, to some degree, by our own experiences as children. Unlike Jenisha, I got a parachute out of my segregated school, and that changed my life. And, as a result, I have always thought about the equal worth of children who didn't get that parachute and how that shaped their lives as well.

"I still believe, as I always have, in public schools as necessary and common good, that education should be the great equalizer and that parents should not have to choose between doing what's right for their children and what's right for community."

Hannah-Jones said the problems raised by both families ultimately required broader policy changes.

"In the end, the inequality I write about and that Jenisha experienced is systemic and will only be fixed if we acquire the political will to make different policy choices that value the inherent worth of all of our children, even if those children happen to be born Black and poor," she said.

MORE THAN 400,000 NEW YORK CITY CHILDREN ENROLLED IN FAILING PUBLIC SCHOOLS: REPORT

School choice advocate Corey DeAngelis, a research fellow at the Heritage Foundation, offered a sharply different assessment in a statement to Fox News Digital, arguing Watts was right to prioritize her son rather than wait for improvements to the public school system.

"Jenisha Watts is doing what a parent is supposed to do. She is putting her son first," he said. "Watts has options most families do not. The scandal is not that she is using them. The scandal is that politicians and teachers unions fight to keep those options out of reach for everyone else. School choice is the equalizer. Trapping kids in failure factories by zip code only makes inequality worse.

"It is time to fund students, not systems, so all families can have a shot at the American dream. If Hannah-Jones and her friends actually want to help other children, they should fight for the funding to follow the student. You do not fix public schools by locking kids in them. You fix them by giving families a way out — and giving those schools a reason to change."

GOV HOCHUL'S PLAN TO OPT NEW YORK INTO FEDERAL SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM DRAWS UNION OPPOSITION

Watts described Hannah-Jones as a "confidant and friend" and defended her against critics who accused her of sacrificing her daughter’s education for her ideals. But Watts said her own childhood in Lexington, Kentucky, where she described receiving an "abysmal education," shaped the choice she is now making for her son.

Watts said those academic deficiencies followed her into adulthood.

"I’m a staff writer for The Atlantic, and I’m writing a memoir, and I still can’t shake off my poor education," she wrote.

KETANJI BROWN JACKSON AGREES WITH MICHELLE OBAMA’S CRITICISM OF ‘PLUCKING’ KIDS OF COLOR INTO ELITE SCHOOLS

The debate followed Hannah-Jones’ recent New York Times Magazine essay revisiting a choice she first detailed in a 2016 Times Magazine cover story. Hannah-Jones said she eventually apologized to her daughter Najya after reviewing academic problems that followed her through elementary and middle school.

Najya told her mother she wished her own education had received more consideration alongside Hannah-Jones’ concerns about educational inequality.

"Sometimes I wish, instead of always thinking about other kids, you would have thought about me. I never really got the education I wanted," Najya said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

New York City Public Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels defended the public school system’s mission in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"From day one, I have made it clear: Every student, regardless of background or ability, should feel affirmed, valued and held to high expectations," Samuels said. "At New York City Public Schools, we know that our students benefit from inclusive environments where every child has access to rigorous academics, student supports and diverse learning opportunities.

"This is the crux of my vision of a truly integrated public school system, and I am committed to doing the work to make that a reality."

Watts said her decision was not meant as a condemnation of Hannah-Jones or parents who choose differently but reflected what she sees as a broader failure that forces families to weigh their children’s immediate interests against struggling schools.

"America should not force parents to make that kind of choice," she said.

item.title: Canadian PM Carney says he was prepared for Trump ordering invasion
item.description: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he weighed the possibility of a U.S. invasion after Trump began calling Canada the 51st state amid tariffs.
item.content:encoded:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he prepared for the "extreme tail risk" that the U.S. would invade Canada amid recent trade tensions.

Carney made the statement in an interview with The New York Times published Wednesday, saying he weighed the possibility after President Donald Trump began referring to Canada as the 51st state.

"I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk. That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case," Carney told the Times, arguing that "it would be irresponsible not to."

CANADIAN PM TELLS TRUMP TO 'STOP TRYING TO BE TOUGH' IN TRADE FIGHT

Trade tensions between the U.S. and Canada have continued to escalate over the past year, with Trump levying increased tariffs and Canada responding in kind.

Carney admitted in a video statement earlier this month that Canada had come to overly rely on its economic relationship with the U.S. in recent decades.

FORMER BIDEN AMBASSADOR BLAMES TRUMP FOR CANADA PLAYING 'FOOTSIE' WITH CHINA

"The past 40 years has been a period of deeper economic integration with the United States. Truth is, it was easy business, but it meant we relied too much on one economic partner. It’s clear that time is over," Carney said.

"This is why our plan, since I came into office, has been development and diversification, not denial, waiting to go back to some good old days and not continued dependence."

FEARS OF A CANADIAN TRADE WAR ARE OVERBLOWN; SO FAR, IT’S MORE OF A SKIRMISH

Trump last week dismissed reports that Canada may be joining the European Union as an associate member, saying the U.S. could impose heavy tariffs on Europe if he believed such a "laughable" move was made with "bad intention."

"I think it's laughable," Trump responded. "If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things.

"If Europe does that with a bad intention — if it's a good intention, that's fine — if it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe."

item.title: Mayday call captures pilot's urgent warning before aircraft goes down off coast
item.description: A Hawker Hunter pilot ejected into the Pacific Ocean after reporting engine failure off California's Central Coast, triggering a dramatic rescue near Morro Bay.
item.content:encoded:
A pilot's dramatic escape from a plane that crashed into the Pacific Ocean off California has prompted an investigation. 

The plane, an MK-58 Hawker Hunter, plunged into the water after the pilot reported trouble while flying off California's Central Coast on Tuesday evening, ABC News reported.

The crash triggered an emergency response near Morro Bay, where the pilot was rescued after ejecting from the aircraft.

DEADLY HELICOPTER CRASH KILLS 2 PILOTS BATTLING RAGING WILDFIRE IN YOSEMITE

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) confirmed to Fox News Digital on Thursday that the plane crashed near San Luis Obispo around 6:50 p.m. after the pilot reported an engine issue.

"Only the pilot was on board," the spokesperson said. "The FAA will investigate."

The Navy has since grounded Hawker Hunters operated by Airborne Tactical Advantage Company (ATAC) while the incident is under investigation, according to ABC News.

The aircraft was being flown in support of a Navy and Marine Corps contract when it went down, according to ABC, citing ATAC.

'WE THOUGHT WE WOULD DIE': PASSENGERS THROWN INTO CEILING DURING TERRIFYING FLIGHT

Four ATAC aircraft, including the one that crashed, were involved in the mission.

Before the crash, the pilot issued a mayday call and reported losing engine thrust, according to air traffic control audio obtained by ABC from LiveATC.net.

"Mayday, mayday, mayday. I have lost thrust in my engine," the pilot told controllers, according to the ABC report.

ATAC operates the aircraft as part of its work supporting training for the U.S. armed forces.

The company has 22 Hawker Hunters in its fleet, according to a Navy public information officer cited by ABC.

The FAA is actively investigating the incident. 

No additional details are known at this time.

In addition, a Delta Air Lines flight recently returned to Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport shortly after takeoff due to a pilot medical emergency.

item.title: Soros-linked prosecutor faces primary challenge as fellow Democrat targets his record
item.description: Fairfax County Commonwealth's Attorney Stephen Descano faces a Democratic primary challenge from a former federal prosecutor citing botched cases.
item.content:encoded:
Fairfax County Commonwealth’s Attorney Stephen Descano is facing a forceful rebuke from a former federal prosecutor who extensively criticized his record after announcing her bid to unseat him.

Descano, a Democrat, has faced criticism over what opponents describe as lenient prosecutorial decisions, particularly in serious cases involving illegal immigrant suspects. Former federal prosecutor Brittany Dunn-Pirio said that if there weren’t systemic problems in his office, she would want to work there.

"If this office were doing its job, I wouldn’t be running against it. I’d be applying to work for it. But it isn’t," Dunn-Pirio said on her new campaign website after Washington, D.C.-area media reported her bid late Wednesday.

VIRGINIA DEMS SPLIT ON DOJ PROBE OF SOROS-BACKED DA ACCUSED OF GIVING 'SWEETHEART DEALS' TO ILLEGAL ALIENS

"I’m a Democrat. This race isn’t about whether reform was right. It’s about whether the office can tell the difference between a first-time nonviolent offender who deserves a second chance and a violent or sexual offender who doesn’t," Dunn-Pirio said on her website.

"It’s about whether deadlines are met, evidence is given to the defendant and victims are spoken to."

VIRGINIA DEM DEFENDS SOROS-BACKED PROSECUTOR FROM DOJ PROBE AFTER ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGING ALLEGATIONS

Fox News Digital reached out to Descano and Dunn-Pirio for further comment.

Descano campaign spokesman Nathan Kiker defended the incumbent's record, telling Fox News Digital that "Steve Descano has spent his tenure proving that you can reform the justice system and keep our community safe at the same time."

"Today, Fairfax County is recognized as the safest large county in the nation because Steve focused on accountability and the root causes of crime rather than failed policies of the past. We are proud to put that record before the voters," Kiker said.

Dunn-Pirio also pointed to "botched sexual assault cases" and prosecutors declining to meet with victims, along with her contention that the justice system too often favors the "well-connected."

One case that has drawn the scrutiny of Descano’s office involves Abdul Jalloh, an illegal immigrant from Sierra Leone charged with murdering Stephanie Minter. Minter was stabbed and killed at a Hybla Valley bus stop in February after Jalloh had cycled through the criminal justice system following numerous previous arrests.

Descano has pushed back on claims that his office simply allowed Jalloh to walk free, telling Congress his prosecutors obtained convictions against him "wherever possible."

SOROS-BACKED DA'S LAX ILLEGAL IMMIGRATION POLICIES LED TO 'PREVENTABLE' BUS STOP STABBING MURDER: COMPLAINT

Dunn-Pirio previously served as a prosecutor in Frederick County, Virginia, and as a federal prosecutor in the district covering Lexington, Kentucky. She said she resigned from the DOJ in 2025 after working on COVID-related fraud and similar cases.

"I couldn’t stomach propping up a system that gave pardons to the well-connected while prosecuting average Americans for the same conduct," she said, according to a release obtained by FairfaxNow.

She also said Descano’s office has spent too much time "failing the people I care about."

A carousel on her new campaign website highlights cases that have drawn public scrutiny of Descano, including:

REPEAT OFFENDER WITH DOZENS OF PRIOR CHARGES ARRESTED FOR BURGLARIZING CHURCH IN SOROS-BACKED DA'S COUNTY

"We need a Commonwealth’s Attorney who can make this office work," Dunn-Pirio said. "Every person in Fairfax should feel safe, and every person in Fairfax should be able to trust the office that’s supposed to protect them."

Descano’s campaign did not immediately respond to an additional request for comment on Dunn-Pirio’s criticism.

Dunn-Pirio, most recently an associate at the civil litigation firm Harman, Claytor, Corrigan & Wellman, served as an assistant U.S. attorney in Kentucky for two years before resigning in November 2025. At the Justice Department, she specialized in COVID relief fraud and public corruption cases, according to her LinkedIn profile.

"Most recently I was a federal prosecutor, and I resigned from the Justice Department because I couldn’t stomach propping up a system that gave pardons to the well-connected while prosecuting average Americans for the same conduct," Dunn-Pirio said.

Before becoming a federal prosecutor in 2023, Dunn-Pirio served as an assistant commonwealth’s attorney in Frederick County, an assistant attorney general in the state criminal appeals courts and a law clerk to Judge Randy Bellows in Fairfax County Circuit Court.

Dunn-Pirio emphasized that she is a "cradle Democrat," distinguishing her candidacy from a challenge to Descano from the political right.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

She said she volunteered for former Vice President Al Gore at age 9, helped lead the College Democrats at the University of Notre Dame, remains active in local Democratic groups and previously managed a campaign for Virginia Del. Marcus Simon, D-Falls Church.

Republicans hold only one seat on the Fairfax County Board of Supervisors, while Democrats hold the remaining seats. Dunn-Pirio’s challenge to Descano will be decided first in the Democratic nomination contest ahead of the 2027 election.

item.title: Why Yankees ace Cam Schlittler is in the AL MVP conversation and could join an exclusive club
item.description: The New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler set a franchise record with 21 starts allowing one or no runs, building his AL MVP and Cy Young case.
item.content:encoded:
If you shoot for the moon, you will land among the stars. In Cam Schlittler’s case, however, he and his blazing fastball may take him past the stars and straight to the moon.

The New York Yankees ace has been nothing short of dominant this season. The swashbuckling 25-year-old is all but a lock to win the American League Cy Young Award.

But why stop there? He should win the American League MVP too. Schlittler should become just the 12th player in MLB history to win the Cy Young and MVP in the same season.

Heading into his final start of the year against the Tampa Bay Rays on Thursday, Schlittler leads all American League pitchers in ERA (1.94) and is tied for first in WHIP with Drew Rasmussen (0.91). He has been durable, making all his starts, and is second in the AL in innings pitched (190 2/3).

With a devastating combination of cutters, sinkers and fastballs, the young right-hander has racked up 234 strikeouts, third in the AL behind Cleveland Guardians ace Gavin Williams (244) and likely Cy Young runner-up Dylan Cease (239).

Schlittler has set a Yankees franchise record by allowing one or no runs in 21 starts this year. He became just the third pitcher age 25 or younger in the live-ball era, which began in 1920, to achieve the feat, joining Dean Chance (1964) and Blake Snell (2018).

Schlittler also leads the AL in bWAR with 7.0, ahead of other MVP contenders such as Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez (6.6), Kansas City Royals star Bobby Witt Jr. (6.5) and Rays phenom Junior Caminero (5.6).

The numbers for Schlittler are outstanding, but they don’t tell the full story.

Schlittler has been the pillar of the Yankees' pitching staff, which leads all of baseball with a 3.21 team ERA.

While the pitching staff has been fantastic, it has have dealt with plenty of injuries to the starting rotation.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Gerrit Cole didn’t make his season debut until May 22, as he was recovering from Tommy John surgery. Carlos Rodón began the season on the IL after undergoing surgery to remove a bone spur and loose bodies and didn’t debut until May 10. That was just his first stint on the IL. He returned to the IL on July 3 and didn’t come back until Aug. 18.

Rodón was not the only Yankees ace to land on the IL twice, as Max Fried did as well. Fried first went on the IL with a left elbow bone bruise on May 13, right after Cole returned, and was activated on July 22. He went on the IL for a second time on Aug. 17 with the same injury and returned Aug. 29.

Ryan Weathers, who had been key in stepping up during the absences of Cole, Fried and Rodón, went on the IL on Aug. 23 with a left forearm flexor strain.

For the Yankees, not only was it paramount that Schlittler make every start, but it was also essential that he remain dominant to help keep the rotation afloat.

Adding to the pressure on Schlittler and the pitching staff as a whole, the Yankees’ offense cratered after Aaron Judge was placed on the IL at the beginning of June. Since June 1, the Yankees have hit a paltry .229 with a putrid .297 on-base percentage.

The Yankees’ offensive ineptitude put further pressure on Schlittler and Co. to win games without Judge.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

In 2023, the Yankees’ season went off the rails when Judge suffered a torn ligament in his toe. They went 25-31 without the captain and missed the postseason. The Yankees’ pitching staff in 2023, led by Cole, who won the AL Cy Young Award that season, had a 3.97 ERA, which was not enough to save the Yankees from finishing 82-80.

In 2026, the Yankees went 48-41 without Judge in the lineup, buoyed by the pitching staff’s excellence. Carried by the Schlittler-led pitching staff, the Yankees made the postseason and secured home-field advantage in the American League Wild Card Series.

While the Yankees didn’t catch the Tampa Bay Rays and win the American League East, they might have missed the postseason entirely if it weren’t for Schlittler.

By the award’s definition, Schlittler has been the most valuable player on his team.

Alvarez has been dominant in his own right. The hulking left-handed hitter, with a .316 batting average, 41 home runs and 102 RBI made a bid for the Triple Crown, but that seems out of reach.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Alvarez has been primarily a designated hitter, filling that role in 131 of the 154 games he played this season. Shohei Ohtani is the only player to win an MVP as a primary designated hitter, and he did so after becoming the first player to hit 50 home runs and steal 50 bases in a season.

Unless Alvarez surges to win the Triple Crown, nothing he is doing this season is unprecedented or historic.

Alvarez’s Astros, who are 78-80, might miss the postseason despite playing in the American League West, a division that has been historically bad.

Bobby Witt Jr. has been his usual superstar self but missed 11 games due to injury and has also taken a slight step back from last season while playing for the AL Central-worst Kansas City Royals.Caminero, the linchpin of the AL-leading Rays’ lineup, trails Schlittler in bWAR by more than a full win. Still, his .274 average and 41 home runs leave him in the thick of the AL MVP race.

Despite the excellence of Alvarez, Witt and Caminero, Schlittler should become the first pitcher since Justin Verlander in 2011 to win the American League MVP.

Verlander, like Schlittler this year, led the American League in bWAR with 8.6.

Without Schlittler, the Yankees do not survive Judge’s absence. When the Yankees could hardly scrape together three runs a game in the dead of summer, Schlittler made sure it was enough to hold on.

Without Schlittler’s dominance and durability, the Yankees do not have the second-best record in the American League (91-67).

Without Schlittler, Yankees fans are in a complete state of panic because they might still be trying to secure a Wild Card berth in a weak American League.

At the sportsbooks, Schlittler is a long shot to win the American League MVP. But odds be damned, the award should be his. He has landed on the moon.

item.title: Devils' new concession contraption lets you play hockey with a popcorn puck while watching actual hockey
item.description: The New Jersey Devils unveiled a branded popcorn bucket featuring a pinball hockey game on top, crafted by Levy Restaurants for stadium concessions.
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever been at a hockey game and thought, "Man, I wish I could be playing some sort of hockey-like game right now with a piece of popcorn as a puck?"

Me neither, but on the off chance that you have, the New Jersey Devils have gone into the lab and made your dream a reality.

Behold! The official Devils-branded popcorn bucket with some kind of pinball hockey game on top!

It's the work of the mad scientists at Levy Restaurants, and it could be the biggest salvo in the ongoing war for novelty stadium concession vessel supremacy.

There's no denying that we live in the golden age of stadium food novelties. From beer sticks, skates, sabres, and horns to small-plastic Zamboni-brand ice resurfacers stuffed full of chicken tenders, it's one of those things that makes you proud to live in the present.

NEW YORK ISLANDERS SET TO UNLEASH CULINARY 'DISASTERPIECE' ON UNSUSPECTING FANS THIS SEASON

I'll take beer skates over rampant tuberculosis and no air conditioning any day.

But this one troubles me a little. It's groundbreaking, but when the goal is to get people watching hockey, why would they need something to entertain them in the stands?

I thought that was the game's job.

Now, I don't have kids — just a dog and a little bit of disposable income — but I would be so annoyed if I bought my youngsters NHL tickets, popcorn at stadium prices in a souvenir bucket, and what do they do?

Ignore the world-class athletes on the ice before them in favor of flippering a piece of Orville Redenbacher's Gourmet popping corn back and forth.

It's like if you needed your kid to stop playing video games to power wash the deck, and when you went to unplug their PlayStation, you realized they were playing "PowerWash Simulator."

Having said that, I feel pretty confident that I would be a very good popcorn hockey player. I just have shockingly quick reflexes and am good enough at geometry to track the bounces when the irregularly shaped popcorn piece hits the boards.

So would I buy one? No, but I'd school anyone who bought one and then sat next to me.

item.title: Macklemore slammed as 'performative' after announcing 'Free Palestine Tour'
item.description: Macklemore announced a "Free Palestine Tour" with shows in Dublin, Paris and London after being dropped from Ed Sheeran's tour over his performances.
item.content:encoded:
Macklemore is taking his views on "Free Palestine" on the road.

The rapper, who was dropped from Ed Sheeran's tour earlier this month after stirring controversy with his politically charged performances, announced Thursday that he's going on a new tour he's calling the "Free Palestine Tour."

"If these last couple of weeks have shown us anything, it’s that something has shifted over the last three years. There has been a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now," he wrote on Instagram.

JAVIER BARDEM SLAMMED FOR TARGETING PINK OVER MACKLEMORE COMMENTS: ‘THE LEFT IS EATING ITSELF’

He continued, "It’s 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore. People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community. To use the stage for more than entertainment. To push back when the call for a Free Palestine is met with attempts to silence it."

Macklemore wrote that "what happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage," and that "when the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention."

He added, "So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit."

He wrote that for the past week, he's been in touch with artists who have also been vocal about their support for Palestinians, "regardless of the consequences" — artists who he says "understand that our platforms mean very little if we’re only willing to use them when it’s safe."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

The "Thrift Shop" rapper also noted that because things are moving so quickly, schedules and details are still being worked out. As of now, he has three shows scheduled: in Dublin on Oct. 26, in Paris on Oct. 29 and in London on Oct. 30.

None of the other performers have been named, but he did state, "All proceeds will benefit organizations supporting the Palestinian people and movement."

The announcement has already made waves, with some critics wondering why he's not performing in the Palestinian territories. One person wrote on social media, "So f---in performative, let's see these 'brave' artists actually go to the countries they're so supportive of."

"If virtual signaling was in the olympics hed get a gold medal," another said.

Others took issue with Macklemore making his music so political, with one X user writing, "I'm pretty sure people just want artists to stfu & do the art....."

Another agreed, saying, "When will celebs learn to stay out of politics? Most of them are vacuous morons who don't know what they're talking about. Sing your little songs and f--- off home. It's not difficult."

READ IT: ED SHEERAN'S PRE-CONCERT SPEECH TO PHILLY CROWD ABOUT THE GAZA CONTROVERSY

"So why he didn’t do it before?" another person asked. "Was it so necessary to involve Ed Sheeran and damage his career? Something fake and sleezy about this guy."

Many people praised Macklemore for his decision to do a tour based on his beliefs.

"Macklemore is nothing but a hero and a role model for all of humanity. so damn proud of him," one fan shared.

"Seriously, mad respect to you for standing up for what you believe. I truly believe we are on the precipice of change and you may have been the bright spark that we needed to set this off," another posted.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Several fans requested that he add more shows, especially in the U.S. cities where he was scheduled to perform before he was dropped from Sheeran's tour.

On Sept. 4, Macklemore opened for Sheeran at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, and he used part of his time onstage to perform his anti-Israel song, "Hind's Hall." He repeatedly chanted "Free Palestine" while a slideshow played on the screen behind him, showing video from the war in Gaza.

WATCH: WHY MACKLEMORE GOT KICKED OFF ED SHEERAN'S TOUR

The controversy surrounding Macklemore's stage appearance continued after the MetLife Stadium performance. He later posted a video on Instagram addressing the crowd and said performing on Sheeran's tour gave him the opportunity to deliver his "Free Palestine" message to a massive audience.

He doubled down in the caption writing, "Wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial."

He was later dropped from the tour altogether after venues told the tour's promoters that they would "not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup."

item.title: Missouri's redistricting mess created an election problem Supreme Court has days to untangle
item.description: The Eighth Circuit ruled Missouri must use its 2025 congressional map for the general election, but the Supreme Court could intervene before Sept. 28.
item.content:encoded:
Missouri’s congressional map fight is hurtling toward another potential Supreme Court showdown, with courts at odds over which districts should govern the November election after more than 1.2 million Missourians voted in the August primary under a different map.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit ruled Monday that Missouri must use its 2025 congressional map in November, finding that switching to the state’s 2022 districts after the primary would violate the U.S. Constitution. But the appeals court paused its order until Sept. 28, 2026, opening a narrow window for another visit to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Abhishek Kambli, a partner at Holtzman Vogel and former deputy associate attorney general at the Justice Department, told Fox News Digital the Supreme Court’s previous intervention does not necessarily signal how the justices will handle the latest ruling.

"It’s unpredictable how they’ll rule, mostly because we didn’t get their reasoning in the last order," Kambli said. "So, we don’t know the precise reason why they decided to stay at that time."

ELECTION CHAOS IN THIS RED STATE JUST GOT EVEN STRANGER FOR REPUBLICANS AFTER SUPREME COURT RULING

The Supreme Court previously stayed a federal district court's temporary restraining order requiring Missouri to use the 2025 map. The Eighth Circuit has now directed the lower court to enter a permanent injunction requiring the newer districts, putting the dispute in a different procedural posture.

"So unless the Supreme Court steps in again, the state will be required to use the seven-one map for this election," Kambli said.

Missouri held its Aug. 4, 2026, primary under the 2025 map. Roughly a month later, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled that voters could challenge the map through a referendum, leaving the 2022 districts in place for the November election.

Kambli said switching congressional maps between the primary and general election raises serious constitutional concerns.

"You would have had a large number of Missourians who would have been disenfranchised because they voted for one set of candidates in the primary and will be voting for another set in the general," Kambli said.

MISSOURI AG FILES PETITION ASKING SUPREME COURT TO REVIVE TRUMP-BACKED REDISTRICTING MAP

"And what's even more concerning is sometimes those candidates are unopposed so that they miss their only chance to vote as a result of what the Missouri Supreme Court did here," Kambli continued. "So that's what's really at issue — is whether everyone gets an equal voice in a situation where the primary election is integral to the electoral system of the state."

But Yale law professor Akhil Amar and University of California, Davis, law professor Vikram Amar have argued the opposite. After the Supreme Court’s earlier stay, Vikram wrote on SCOTUSblog that using the 2025 map in November would not protect anyone’s right to vote if those lines were never legally in effect. Akhil agreed with his analysis.

"HB1’s district lines lack the force of law, full stop," Vikram wrote. "These lines cannot be used wrongly in November just because they were previously used wrongly in the primary. Two wrongs do not make (or vindicate) a right (to vote)."

Meanwhile, Kambli placed much of the blame for the eleventh-hour legal scramble over which map to use on the Missouri Supreme Court, arguing the turmoil was "entirely preventable."

VIRGINIA GOP, DEMS BATTLE IT OUT OVER REDISTRICTING BEFORE STATE SUPREME COURT

Kambli argued that the Missouri Supreme Court could have resolved the map dispute earlier, noting that the issue remained unsettled even after the candidate filing deadline passed.

Alicia Bannon, senior director of the Judiciary Program at the Brennan Center for Justice, pointed instead to delays by Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins as a key reason the dispute dragged on.

Opponents of the 2025 map submitted more than 300,000 signatures in December 2025, but Hoskins did not formally reject the referendum petition until Aug. 4, the day of the primary.

"Time passed. And passed further," Bannon wrote for State Court Report. "As early as December 2025, Hoskins asserted in separate federal litigation that a referendum on redistricting was not authorized by the state constitution. But he held off on issuing a certificate on that basis — which would have triggered judicial review — instead going through a lengthy process of verifying petition signatures."

Bannon wrote that the Missouri Supreme Court’s criticism of Hoskins’ delays stood out, particularly the court’s rejection of his argument that it had waited too long to intervene.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

The Missouri Supreme Court ultimately ruled that the referendum could proceed and faulted Hoskins for the delay, saying he had "created the confusion, expense, and practical difficulties of which he complains."

Kambli argued the Purcell principle, under which federal courts generally avoid changing election rules close to Election Day because of the potential for disruption, weighs in favor of keeping the 2025 map because Missouri already used it for the primary.

"The Eighth Circuit said that the Purcell principles support the injunction, not go against it," Kambli said.

Bannon also warned that courts being too cautious can create its own problems.

"It’s an approach that’s understandable in some circumstances but can also incentivize shenanigans to evade judicial review while harming voters’ rights," Bannon wrote.

Bannon suggested earlier court action in Missouri could have helped avoid the last-minute dispute, including by moving the primary or setting a firm deadline for the referendum petition.

But regardless of whether the Supreme Court decides to weigh in, the referendum will still be on the ballot.

"If the Supreme Court does not stay the Eighth Circuit injunction, there's no doubt that the 7-1 map is what will be in effect for this election. There's still going to be a referendum on the ballot deciding that issue for future elections, but for this one, that's how it'll be decided," Kambli said.

item.title: While Millennials cheer Toys R Us comeback, key piece of data reveals dystopian reason for its return
item.description: Toys R Us plans to open 120 new stores this holiday season, but surging adult toy sales among millennials are driving the iconic retailer's comeback.
item.content:encoded:
If you came of age in the 80s or 90s, chances are you remember Toys R Us, the international toy retailer with the anthropomorphic giraffe for a mascot and the catchiest jingle in the business.

"I don't wanna grow up, I wanna be a Toys R Us kid."

Well, the truth of the matter is we did grow up, and about a decade ago, millennials aging out of the toy-buying demographic spelled doom for the once-titanic toy store, as Toys R Us filed for bankruptcy in 2017 and closed all of their stores the following year.

'TOY STORY 5' REVIEW: TOM HANKS, TIM ALLEN RETURN FOR TIMELY INSTALLMENT AS PIXAR GANG BATTLES RISE OF TECH

But then, just recently, something unexpected happened.

Toys R Us started to make a comeback, first as a part of larger retail stores like Macy's, and then, little by little, as standalone shops in malls and airports.

THE NINTENDO 64 IS TURNING 30 YEARS OLD, HERE ARE SOME OF ITS MOST IMPACTFUL GAMES OF ALL TIME

Now, Toys R Us is set to open 120 stores across the country this holiday season, bringing its total number of standalone U.S. stores to 160.

Hang on just a second, though. Did you read the last part of that post?

"As toy sales surge among adult shoppers," reads like there are a bunch of losers in their 30s and 40s pacing up and down the aisles of their local toy stores while shoving kids out of the way for the last Funko Pop.

But surely that's not the case here, right? This is just a bunch of older Millennials with kids of their own passing on their love of toys and games to the next generation.

Right?

Yep, I knew it.

It looks like the only reason Toys R Us is making a comeback is because a bunch of 90s kids who are now old enough to have kids of their own took that aforementioned jingle a little too literally.

I know you "wanna be a Toys R Us kid," but you're 36 years old. It's time to let someone a little younger have a crack at the LEGO Star Wars set.

I don't know what it is with my generation and having a serious case of arrested development, but they're almost allergic to acting their age.

Listen, I'm not saying you're not allowed to have some of the same hobbies you had when you were 13.

WE GREW UP BEFORE SCREENS TOOK OVER. OUR KIDS DESERVE THAT CHANCE TOO

Hell, I will still hop on the Xbox to blow off a little steam or watch movies and TV shows from my youth.

But I also haven't been spending chunks of my salary on toys and video games for most of my adult life, and I donated all my Pokemon cards to kids at the summer camp I used to work at back in college.

If I have bought a toy in the past two years, it was for my son, and that's the disheartening thing about these numbers.

Instead of passing the "kid hobbies" torch, Millennials are just hoarding it to themselves.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Nostalgia is a powerful agent, one that I have been known to write about frequently, but there's a fine line between showing reverence for "the good old days" and outright refusing to live in the present.

It's a ton of fun to see my son's eyes light up whenever he opens the package to a Spider-Man figure or a Bluey plushy, but I couldn't imagine someone with a beard and a car payment getting the same satisfaction from that.

It all feels weird and a little dystopian.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

I'll be excited to take my son to Toys R Us when one opens near me, just as my dad did when I was a kid, but the joy will be vicarious.

Anything more than that just wouldn't feel right.

item.title: Ms Rachel defends her activism by pointing to Mister Rogers' political legacy on children's TV
item.description: Children's YouTube star Ms. Rachel cited Fred Rogers' civil rights pool scene and nuclear arms race episodes to defend her own political activism.
item.content:encoded:
Children's YouTube personality Ms. Rachel hit back at critics of her political activism during an interview Tuesday, pointing to Mister Rogers, who she said was very political.

Ms. Rachel, whose full name is Rachel Griffin Accurso, spoke to Kareem Rahma, host of "SubwayTakes," and broke down her hottest takes.

"Mr. Rogers was political," she said. Mister Rogers, whose full name was Fred Rogers, is known for "Mister Rogers' Neighborhood," a children's program that ran from 1968-2001.

MS RACHEL CLAIMS CELEBRITIES SILENT ON GAZA WOULD ‘PROBABLY’ SPEAK IF CHILDREN ‘WERE WHITE’

Ms. Rachel pointed to an example in the children's show in which Rogers invited Officer Clemmons, a Black character, to cool off in a small wading pool during the civil rights movement. The episode aired in 1969, at a time when some public pools still prohibited Black swimmers.

Rahma called the episode "revolutionary."

YOUTUBE STAR MS RACHEL DECLARES 'I AM POLITICAL' IN NEW MISSION TO SHUT DOWN ICE FACILITY

"I've read that some people saw it and in their family it wasn't okay to share a pool, and they were like, 'Oh Mr. Rogers is doing it. It's okay for our family now.' And so it did make a difference and actually, people sometimes say to me or, you know, in the media, they'll be like, ‘Ms. Rachel should be like Mister Rogers and not be political.' And actually, he was political so much on the show. I think maybe they didn't watch it or maybe weren't paying attention because he did so many things," Ms. Rachel said.

Ms. Rachel also pointed to a series of episodes from 1983, telling Rahma that Rogers was against the nuclear arms race.

"He was against the nuclear arms race, and he had, in his neighborhood make-believe, he had King Friday building bombs because he thought the other neighborhood, Southwood, was building bombs, so he wanted to have 100 million and one bomb parts for his bombs and in the show. And then he was like, 'Now we don't have money for the music program because you spent it all on bombs. Queen Sarah, the wife, was like, ‘Why did you spend the tax money on bombs? We should have spent it on these other awesome things,’" Ms. Rachel said.

She noted that Mister Rogers also testified before the Senate in support of funding for public broadcasting.

"Nixon wanted to cut $10 million from the PBS budget, and he testified in front of the Senate, and he just shared from his heart how much care goes into his show and how he helps children manage, and feelings are manageable and mentionable, and it was huge and the very like-grrrrrr Senate guy was like, ‘You got your $20 million.’ And it was so touching. It's like the coolest video," Ms. Rachel said.

She added, "And so he went to Senate and was like, 'No, government, don't cut funding to PBS.' Like, how political is that?"

MS RACHEL CLAIMS 'NO ONE NEEDS A BILLION DOLLARS,' ENDORSES DEMOCRATIC PROGRESSIVES ABDUL EL-SAYED, CORI BUSH

Author and psychotherapist Jonathan Alpert told Fox News Digital in a statement, "Fred Rogers addressed serious social issues. His 1969 pool scene with Officer Clemmons was a powerful statement about racial equality. But there’s a difference between quietly modeling human dignity and turning your enormous platform with children and parents into a vehicle for your positions on today's political controversies."

Alpert continued, "Rogers didn't need to tell his audience, 'Here is the correct political position.' He showed a Black neighbor that he was welcome in his pool. The lesson was contained in the act itself. Ms. Rachel is far more explicit about telling the public what she believes about Gaza, immigration and other politically charged issues. I think invoking Mister Rogers gives her a convenient defense: If Mister Rogers was political, then criticism of her activism can be dismissed as hypocrisy. But that's a false equivalence. You can admire what Rogers did in 1969 without concluding that every children's entertainer therefore has a mandate to become a political activist."

YOUTUBE STAR MS RACHEL GIVES FUNDS TO DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED

ROSIE O’DONNELL RANTS THAT TRUMP-ERA ICE FACILITIES ARE CONCENTRATION CAMPS WHERE INMATES ARE RAPED

Alpert said Rogers was "influential precisely because he didn't beat people over the head with his politics."

"He trusted the audience to understand the lesson. The pool scene didn't come with a lecture or a list of political demands. He showed people how to behave," Alpert said of Mister Rogers.

Fred Rogers Productions did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Ms. Rachel's other takes included one about children in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.

"No child should be in immigration detention center ever," she said. "I've talked with some children, and the harm is so obvious."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"And we don't want to be people who abuse children. It's the medical neglect is abuse. So, they're actually abusing children. And some pediatricians I've talked to have even said torture. Some autistic children in there, like keeping the lights on 24 hours, just that they've been unable to go to the bathroom, to poop for nine days. And as parents, it's like, that's so wrong. Like you can't, and there was a girl they neglected that she had this respiratory stuff, and when they took her to the ICU, she had COVID, RSV. Her oxygen was like 52. So the medical neglect is abuse in there," Ms. Rachel said.

ICE did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

item.title: Lane Kiffin caught lying about LSU-Ole Miss series while complaining about nine-game SEC schedule
item.description: Lane Kiffin can't stop complaining about SEC schedule quirks ahead of LSU's crucial matchup against Marcel Reed and Texas A&M in Baton Rouge.
item.content:encoded:
LSU welcomes a Top 25 Texas A&M team to Baton Rouge on Saturday in what is being viewed as a make-or-break game between the two one-loss teams, but Tigers head coach Lane Kiffin can't seem to stop talking about his team's loss at Ole Miss.

During Wednesday's SEC coaches' teleconference call, Kiffin spoke about the challenges of his team taking on another dual-threat quarterback this week in Texas A&M's Marcel Reed after struggling to slow down Ole Miss star Trinidad Chambliss.

Or at least that's what his comments were initially focused on before complaining about his team's schedule.

LANE KIFFIN SUGGESTS OLE MISS BROKE RULES WITH IN-STADIUM MUSIC DURING LSU'S LOSS TO REBELS

"Obviously we just played the best one in the country last week thinking he can hurt you even when you have the right call on and everybody covered and a guy comes free," Kiffin explained. "Obviously he (Chambliss) played great a year ago here in the stadium, so this is one of those scheduling quirks just like last week where never in that LSU-Ole Miss series had it ever been played two times in a row."

While it is both odd and rare that Ole Miss got the benefit of playing LSU – a historic rival – in Oxford back-to-back seasons, Kiffin's claim that the series had never been played at the same venue in consecutive seasons is false.

item.title: US allies need to shoot down Russian aircraft testing NATO boundaries, Czech president warns
item.description: Czech President Petr Pavel warned NATO may need to shoot down Russian aircraft or drones deliberately violating allied airspace to avoid weakness.
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Czech President Petr Pavel insists that NATO needs to outright demonstrate its willingness to respond to Russian aggression or else Moscow will continue to push the alliance and its European boundaries.

"There might be the time when we will have to shoot down some of these planes or unmanned vehicles that are testing our readiness," Pavel, a retired general and former chair of NATO's Military Committee, predicted in a conversation with Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York City this week.

Pavel said alliance members understandably want to avoid escalation, but risk sending the wrong signal as he warned Moscow views restraint as weakness and is testing allied defenses with its continued aggression.

"What I am afraid of is that they see a lack of will on our side to take decisive action," Pavel said. "Within Russian perceptions it demonstrates weakness. And they respect power."

The warning followed fresh incidents along NATO’s eastern flank, where a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter crossed from Kaliningrad into Polish airspace Wednesday, prompting Poland to scramble fighter jets. Romania scrambled F-16s Thursday after another unidentified aerial target crossed its border from Ukraine.

Denmark’s military intelligence service also warned Thursday that Russia is likely to intensify hybrid attacks against NATO in the coming months and assessed a "low but growing" risk of a limited Russian military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.

ROMANIAN F-16 SHOOTS DOWN DRONE AFTER AIRSPACE BREACH, MARKING FIRST FOR NATO ALLY

Pavel said in a speech before the U.N. General Assembly Wednesday that Russia's "aggressive posture poses a direct threat to European security" and warned that the risk is growing.

He told Fox News Digital that the pattern of recent escalation was familiar from his years at NATO, recalling Russian aircraft testing U.S. pilots over Syria and repeatedly violating Turkish airspace before Turkey shot down a Russian warplane in 2015.

"They are, on one hand, provoking. On the other, testing what will our reaction be," Pavel detailed.

NATO already has procedures for accidental airspace violations, Pavel said, including warning aircraft and attempting to establish contact. But he drew a distinction between mistakes and aircraft that deliberately enter allied airspace and refuse to respond.

"If it is deliberate and the violator doesn’t respond to our measures, then we will have to act, because otherwise Russia simply would push further on," the Czech president added.

RUSSIA'S NEIGHBOR REVEALS PERSONAL APPEALS TO TRUMP AS US WEIGHS NATO TROOP PULLBACK IN EUROPE

The comments come amid recent drone incursions involving NATO members along the alliance’s eastern flank, including incidents in Poland, Romania and Lithuania.

Pavel was similarly skeptical that President Vladimir Putin is serious about talks to end the war in Ukraine, saying he has seen no significant Russian effort to negotiate. He argued that while Moscow publicly expresses willingness to hold talks, the conditions it has attached would effectively strip Ukraine of sovereignty.

He said a genuine negotiating process would require Russia to agree to a ceasefire first and then enter talks without preconditions.

RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS

The Czech president also warned that the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have exposed another vulnerability across the NATO alliance: depleted weapons stockpiles and defense-production systems struggling to keep pace with demand.

"With the amount of ammunition, especially intelligent ammunition, consumed over a short period of time, we all understand on both sides of the Atlantic how short we are when it comes to stocks of these kinds of equipment," Pavel said.

He said the lesson for both Europe and the United States is to accelerate weapons production and overhaul procurement systems he described as "extremely long and rigid."

Pavel’s warning underscores a broader challenge facing NATO as it weighs how forcefully to respond to Russian activity without triggering a wider confrontation, while simultaneously replenishing the military stockpiles needed to sustain deterrence over the longer term.

item.title: Dem Senate hopeful rocked by explosive ex-aide claims as campaign cites ‘hardest period of her life’
item.description: Mary Peltola says her alleged outbursts came amid grief after losing her mother and husband months apart, pushing back on the New York Times report.
item.content:encoded:
Former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska, is facing allegations from former aides that she erupted in anger, used offensive slurs, sent profane text messages and once shoved a staffer — claims her campaign disputes while denying that they reflect a broader pattern of abusive behavior.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that former Peltola aides alleged she was quick to anger, used anti-gay slurs and a slur targeting the mentally handicapped, sent edgy text messages and, in one case, shoved an employee. Though Peltola’s campaign disputed several of the allegations, her spokesman said some of her behavior came during a period of extreme grief after the deaths of her mother and husband in 2023.

"Mary suddenly and tragically lost both her mother and her husband in the span of a few months in 2023. At the time of their passing, Mary was parenting kids through their own grief, serving full-time in the U.S. House of Representatives thousands of miles from home, and running a competitive re-election campaign – all while shouldering the enormous burden of grief," a spokesman for her campaign told the media in response to the report. 

FETTERMAN LEANS ON UNLIKELY GOP ALLY AS DEMS SHARPEN THEIR KNIVES OVER EXPLOSIVE REPORT

"Like any person who has gone through multiple personal tragedies in the span of a few months, Mary sometimes struggled to deal with her grief. But she treats her staff with respect and care, and she maintains close positive relationships with her staff spanning her nearly 30 years in public service," the spokesman continued. "Exaggerating and outright lying about moments from the hardest period of her life, and falsely presenting them as a pattern of behavior, is wrong."

Peltola avoided reporters’ questions about the allegations after a Wednesday town hall, leaving without responding, Alaska News Source reported.

While much of the behavior described in the New York Times article, such as Peltola’s alleged use of slurs and the shove, occurred during the aftermath of her personal tragedies, other incidents purportedly happened more recently.

The atmosphere in Peltola’s congressional office allegedly drove aides to tears and prompted discussions about quitting, with some saying the stress caused them to lose weight or seek therapy, according to the New York Times. The outlet separately described anxiety and exhaustion among staff on her 2026 Senate campaign.

BAD BOSSES ON CAPITOL HILL COULD FACE RECKONING UNDER NEW ANONYMOUS STAFFER REVIEW PLATFORM

Some commentators from across the political spectrum defended Peltola or questioned the significance of some of the allegations.

"I think most reasonably well-adjusted people would read this and feel pretty sympathetic toward Peltola rather than her annoying staffers," left-of-center pollster Nate Silver said of the reporting. A Democratic communications staffer noted that getting yelled at by your boss is relatively normal on the Hill.

"Call me crazy, but I do not think it's very objectionable for Mary Peltola, who commutes from Alaska to Washington DC, to ask a staffer to feed her pet," Robby Soave, who writes for a libertarian magazine, said.

Not everyone took the Senate hopeful’s side, however.

"Mary Peltola has a problem with violence and aggression, and she doesn't deserve to be dog-catcher let alone a U.S. Senator. Mary should apologize for her unhinged behavior," Republican National Committee spokesman Nick Poche said of the reporting.

"I thought Peltola was boring and useless until I read this," former Rep. Matt Gaetz wrote on X. "Was this leaked to help Peltola with Alaskan men?"

Staffers complained to the New York Times about having to feed live crickets to Peltola's pet chameleon, Meatball. Some of the staffers who complained about the working conditions in Peltola’s congressional office returned to work for her Senate campaign.

DEM SENATE HOPEFUL VOWS TO UNLEASH ALASKA OIL — BUT HER RECORD TELLS A DIFFERENT STORY

Peltola and incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan are the leading contenders in Alaska’s four-candidate general election for U.S. Senate, which will likely be one of the closest Senate elections of this cycle. Though traditionally a red state, shifting voter preferences combined with Peltola’s unique crossover appeal have put Alaska in play for the Democrats.

Peltola’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday.
